title: Jonathan Lessard - A Simulation with a View
speaker: Jonathan Lessard
description:
Roguelike systems are often full of rich, intricately generated environmental and historical details. Most of it is lost on players who typically navigate the world through the perspective of a single or small party of adventurers. This makes sense in terms of aligning player and character perspective in their journey. It does, however, limit the information they have access to in terms of discovering interesting or quirky emergent details and stories.

Our current project takes the opposite stance of exposing as much of the simulation as possible to allow players the fun of perusing and discovering the intricacies of its generated histories. This led to a series of novel design problems: how to present this massive quantity of information? And how to give players reasons to engage with it.

In this quick talk, I will quickly explain our approaches to tackling these issues. First, I will present our Chroniqueur interface which affords players an immediate, accessible Wikipedia-like interface documenting most of the world’s simulated history. Secondly, I will touch on the Divine Affaire gameplay which positions players as higher entities responding to the needs of simulated characters. To devise wise plans of actions, they first need to investigate the simulated lives and understand the given situations. Given the complexity of the simulation, miraculous meddling does not always yield the expected results and much of the fun comes from uncovering the consequences of one’s interventions in the characters’ timelines.

last is design affairs. There are angles to this project that I find are possibly
interesting for both roguelike players and roguelike developers. Hopefully that will
be true. The title is "A Simulation with a View." Hopefully it will make sense soon.
We start from this assumption that many roguelikes have an underlying simulation.
To a different extent but some of them have an intense simulation thinking of Dwarf Fortress,
for example, crusader kings and the Sims. When I began on this project, it was building a complex
social simulation was one of my starting points. This was my view a few years ago of trying to
figure out what was happening under the hood. Tons of stuff is happening as simulations do. You
know, in my case, I also had some intentions in terms of what I wanted to model. I wanted
to try to model the social conditions that led to the newly thick revolution in the sore story
of humans and the history of humans and I am not sure I achieved it but at least I informed myself
as to social and ecological mechanisms and stuff like that. The truth is most of that is unseen.
My first big question is how will people know about all that? I am sure that resonates to some
of you. You have complex systems but exposing them is a challenge actually. Typical approach
to roguelikes is you have a game view meaning exposure is through what you are paying attention
to and the information you get and the actions you are undertaking. That's what you can see.
Obviously you can't know or pay attention to what's outside your game view. Tons of stuff
is missing from your attention which is not an issue. It is design on purpose because the
positioning of the player as a limited awareness is definitely part of the game. But we could
imagine something else. There is also the issue of all this stuff that I missed in the past,
things all happen in the present. And if I miss something, then it is buried somewhere and I can't
necessarily access as it. That's all lost. Pay attention to what happened in the simulation.
So my intuition was first what if everything was documented? Training as a historian and
definitely have a fantasy if the world was all completely objectively documented in some huge
archive that would be really interesting. I didn't make this up. I have these inspirations
in mind when I started doing this. So the Dwarf Fortress legend mode is a big one. James Ryan's
work in general but in particular diety which outputs the whole simulation as a series of
web pages and to me that's interesting. This is what the game looks like and this
is like the game view. The new and different thing I want to introduce to you is these ideas
of chronicles. In this game, at any given moment, you can click on the chronicles down there, and
you have access to something like as exhaustive as possible Wikipedia of the world. This is live
meaning if you move forward in the game all of the information is updated. People who are live are
now dead and you can get graphs, for example, in the world page. I can see the fluctuations
in the human population should attract my attention to something happened here and maybe
I should dig deeper and find out. Every person and character in the game has their own Wikipedia page
with biography, current situation, even their face and information is there. It has multiple
tabs. You can look at families. This person has a husband right now but two ex-husbands so I could
be curious as to what happened to them. They died? Died of what? What age were they? I can see there
are children here and looking at the different last names I see that possibly of different
marriages so my curiosity can be aroused here. For each character, I have the full timeline of their
life. All simulated events are reported year by year with hyperlinks so for example on the year,
151 that character found a new mate. No, that's the person who was introduced to the new mate
and I can click on the new mate and find out about them. And then a bunch of other things happened
that year of either sometimes of importance and sometimes trivial in nature but it is there.
This is my view to the simulation. The chronicles give me all this. Most game objects can generate
graphs. For example, this character had a big uptake in influence, social influence somewhere
around the year 116-117. Once again, maybe a lead to go figure out this story here of what happened
and why did they lose influence. I could also cross reference values and stuff like that.
Which leads me to the other issue. There is a lot of information being generated. That information
is now accessible and to some extent parseable and legible. It is not hard to figure out. But the big
question now is why would people/players care about all that information? All these fictional
people living or dead and all the minor details of their lives? A big issue I don't claim to
have an answer to this. The main approach that games have is to create a game around
it. When you first made a game where you played one character in there but the lives of the NPCs
are not all that interesting so we -- I mean, it is unlikely that the one character will be
interesting. But we thought it is kind of likely if you could look at many characters at once,
or had reasons to look at many characters, then you could find out possibly interesting emergent
stories in there, so we were designing design affair as a God game but you play one of the
numerous gods in the simulation and as everything else in the simulations these Gods are part of the
simulation. They are created by groups of people, communities, as protector gods, and then they are
living in a relationship of reciprocal service where believers of these gods endue them with
energy but in response the gods are expected to fulfill the believer's desires or ambitions. God
has its own page. It is not super sexy right now. This one big story. They are currently associated
to chins and the ritual is to celebrate them by decorating a severe song. But the fun thing is
people communicate through prayers. For example, Jessica is in love with Valerie and says if you
make this happen she will sacrifice food for you but if you don't she will be disappointed and make
that disappointment known to her peers. You have to do it or at least she expects you to do it.
You have a reason to explore the situation. I find out these two people are actually pretty far away.
That might be one of the problems. Maybe worse is one of them is definitely attracted to the other
but the other not really. So that's an issue. But if I look deeper, I see that one of them -- that
Jessica has been pretty active in trying to seduce Valerie. I mean, it seems to be not working too
bad. At least progress is happening. Valerie blushes as she listens to the poetry I compose
in her name so it is going maybe not too bad. Whoops. I skipped one. Maybe what I can do is
I will move and intervene in the simulation by acting miracles. You have a bunch of possible
miracles that you can do. The thing here I decide I can do is at least move one of them to the other
place and see what happens. But of course I am taking responsibility for this because, I mean,
Valerie especially didn't ask for anything. So who am I to mess with her life? So I decided to move
Jessica and induce her to travel the world and go at the same place as Valerie but the outcome was
that she did move there and then I can look at this incentive to look at the aftermath or what

might be an interesting turnout. I am stopping here because you see the point. But the idea is
that if instead of being a single player or small group of player, having a top-down view in the
game as a role, then you have this opportunity and incentive to go explore the details of that
story. All right. I will stop here. Thank you and hopefully there is some questions.
